clarity.justification: The procedure is logically aligned with the hypothesis: it will "fit linear probes," apply "minimal-norm activation edits," and compare the resulting output change with a "theory-predicted response curve," while random-direction and shuffled-label edits provide relevant comparisons. The prediction that "a minority of decodable scientific concepts pass" is directional, so a majority passing would refute it, but "pass" has no numerical fidelity threshold and "mechanistic-fidelity = realized/predicted variance" is underspecified regarding sign, uncertainty, and near-zero predicted variance. Moreover, examples such as a "known logP-solubility slope" do not by themselves define a scientifically valid causal counterfactual because such relationships can be approximate and confounded, a problem the claim acknowledges when it says that defining the response curve "requires modeling assumptions."

feasibility.justification: The hardest step is to "compare to the theory-predicted response curve" across heterogeneous scientific domains; this requires custom scientific modeling rather than a magic operation, but the plan does not specify how the curves or their uncertainty will be constructed. Linear probes and "minimal-norm activation edits" are standard operations supported by common ML and interpretability tooling, and molecular-property, materials, protein, and physics-forecasting model classes exist, although the proposal names no particular models, datasets, layers, or released checkpoints whose compatibility can be checked. Resources are only minimally quantified as "four models and one well-defined mechanistic variable each," with no sample sizes, model scales, intervention counts, or evaluation-set sizes. The refuting branch is runnable because "random-direction edits, label-shuffled probe directions, and non-minimal edits" are explicit controls that can reveal absent or nonspecific effects, though no on-manifold or matched-perturbation control directly resolves the acknowledged off-target-edit confound.
